item.title: Quantum manifestations of converse symmetry breaking
item.description: arXiv:2610.40762v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Quantum synchronization holds promise in advancing quantum technologies such as sensing, communication, and computation. A key challenge in this rapidly developing field is to identify mechanisms that can promote the emergence of synchronous dynamics. Here, we show that quantum synchronization can be enhanced by introducing controlled heterogeneity in the form of coupling mismatches. Using spin van der Pol oscillators as a model system, we show that this mechanism constitutes a quantum analog of the phenomenon of converse symmetry breaking previously identified in classical oscillator networks, where a synchronous state is stabilized by explicit symmetry breaking. We quantify how quantum effects modify this behavior by tuning the degree of quantumness through variations of the spin quantum number. These findings suggest that quantum synchronization can be enhanced in experiments by harnessing rather than suppressing heterogeneity.
item.dc:creator: Daniel P. Buser, Biswabibek Bandyopadhyay, Adilson E. Motter

item.title: Metastable states are precursors of Turing patterns in Adaptive Networks
item.description: arXiv:2611.28828v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In networked reaction-diffusion systems, emergence of patterns from a homogeneous equilibrium can be described by Turing instability. Recently, Turing theory has been developed to include adaptive networks where, i.e., link weights change as a function of the states of the nodes. In this work we show that metastable states, defined as long living transient epochs with unique dynamical properties, could be observed in a range of parameters between Turing patterns and absence of any spatial pattern. Stated differently in the metastable regime the system ''switches'' between the homogeneous solution and the Turing pattern, never settling in any of those states, i.e., alternating silent and spiking regimes. By using phase diagrams and recurrence plots, we have numerically shown the existence of metastable states for the Brusselator model. Moreover, the dependence of the emergence of the metastable states on the adaptive control parameter has been characterized. The applicability of methods and ideas proposed in this work go beyond the considered case, they can help us in understanding conditions under which metastable states arise and could thus be informative to predict and control the latter.
item.dc:creator: S. Nirmala Jenifer, Timoteo Carletti

item.title: Collective order from language models without communication, memory or shared context
item.description: arXiv:2611.30521v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Physical matter orders without a centre: units interact only with neighbours, and fluctuations carry them over energy barriers from a locally stable arrangement to the ordered state. We ask whether language-model agents can do the same, treating each memoryless query as a particle that sees its neighbours but cannot communicate, has no identifier or shared context and receives the same question as all others. Such a particle behaves as if at zero temperature: told a rule or a temperature, it returns the most probable state, and a collective can freeze in a local minimum. We therefore give each particle only a goal and a die whose weights it sets itself, and test several models. Some of them use the die as a noise source even at a local optimum, with weights that fall with the energy cost of the move; on a lattice the energy of one of them climbs over barriers and reaches the ground state, where the noise stops by itself. Particles in three-lane counterflow also order, from mixed traffic into one-way lanes: a spontaneous symmetry breaking. Decentralized collective order can thus arise from disorder without communication, memory or shared context, with noise that the particles choose themselves.
item.dc:creator: Yong Wang

item.title: Impact of Channel Dynamics on Higher-order Interactions of Oscillators
item.description: arXiv:2607.07662v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Modeling higher-order interactions (HOIs) in nonlinear networks with static topologies is often physically restrictive. We demonstrate that standard 3-body Kuramoto couplings are mathematically equivalent to pairwise connections modulated by latent variables of transmission channels. While standard HOI topologies emerge in the adiabatic limit of these variables, relaxing this constraint reveals that latent channel timescales dictate collective macroscopic states. Specifically, transmission inertia drives bistability for symmetric interaction tensors and anti-phase cluster synchronization for antisymmetric ones. Furthermore, dynamically induced clustering in global topologies emerges as a finite-size effect of the dynamics of the local channels. Ultimately, we show that relying exclusively on static topologies restricts interaction modeling. Integrating latent variables captures the transient inertia and fundamental asymmetry of physical networks, bridging the analytical utility of higher-order functions with the reality of the underlying transmission medium.
item.dc:creator: Gabriel Marghoti, Isabela A. Martins, Giovana S. Spezzatto, Emanuel B. S. A. Cambraia, Sergio R. Lopes, Thiago L. Prado

item.title: Fluctuating resource availability stabilizes coexistence beyond the oscillatory tragedy of the commons
item.description: arXiv:2611.06156v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Fluctuations in ambient conditions such as temperature and humidity can alter the effective availability of a shared resource at a given abundance. Standard evolutionary games with environmental feedback treat the payoff matrix as a deterministic function of resource abundance, leaving open how fluctuations in availability affect the oscillatory tragedy of the commons. Using noise-corrected replicator dynamics and individual-based birth-death simulations, we show that zero-mean fluctuations in resource availability can stabilize an interior equilibrium and suppress coupled strategy-resource oscillations. We derive an analytical criterion, in terms of the payoff structure and feedback dynamics, for when increasing noise favors local stability. These findings identify environmental variability as a mechanism that can promote strategy coexistence and help maintain shared resources in systems prone to recurrent depletion.
item.dc:creator: Yi-Duo Chen, Jian-Yue Guan, Zhi-Xi Wu

item.title: From description to design: Automated engineering of complex systems with desirable emergent properties
item.description: arXiv:2603.15631v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Across the sciences, researchers have developed hundreds of statistics that describe the collective behavior of complex systems. These statistics are typically used passively, to describe a system after the fact, so it is rarely learned whether the patterns captured actually matter. The problem of engineering systems that display desirable emergent properties is a less developed area, as the very nature of emergent phenomena challenges the typical bottom-up approach to engineering. Here we propose a top-down approach, re-purposing the large number of descriptive statistics as objective functions in an optimization pipeline. Since this method lets a collective property instantiated directly, it makes long-standing correlational questions amenable to experimentation. We demonstrate this concept on four models taken from four different areas of science: a Kuramoto coupled-oscillator model (physics), a Wilson-Cowan network of excitatory and inhibitory processes (neuroscience), an SIRS pandemic spread model (epidemiology), and an echo-state network (machine learning). In each case, we take measures commonly used to describe behavior and feed those descriptive statistics back into the system to sculpt desirable macro-scale properties into the fundamental generative dynamics. We find that this approach is successful across domains and systems, and the inclusion of ``emergent" measures can actually improve the ability of some systems to perform tasks. We argue these threads can be unified into a general practice of emergent engineering that combines traditional task-oriented, bottom-up approaches to engineering with top-down guidance of collective, emergent properties to build resilient, capable, complex systems.
item.dc:creator: Thomas F. Varley, Josh Bongard

item.title: Growing Hypergraphs with Homophily
item.description: arXiv:2607.16046v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: There are many extant models of hypergraphs with interactions governed by attribute-based homophily between nodes, but most assume independence between edges conditional on node parameters. Relaxing this assumption, we study a mechanistic model of growing hypergraphs in which edge formation is influenced by both previous edges and binary node labels. Edges form in this model as noisy copies of previous edges, where the transmission of nodes from one edge to the next depends on multiple homophilic mechanisms between labels. These homophilic mechanisms give rise to tunable assortative structure in the hypergraph. We derive a power law for the degree distribution in this model and describe the long-term dynamics of the joint distribution of labels contained in edges. Our model defines a likelihood over a labeled hypergraph, allowing us to use standard maximum-likelihood techniques to structure algorithms. We estimate the model parameters on synthetic and real data via (stochastic) expectation maximization. These estimates give statistically-principled descriptions of the operation of homophily in empirical polyadic systems. We also demonstrate an approach to community detection via simulated annealing which, though computationally expensive, achieves competitive results on both synthetic data and certain empirical data sets known to be challenging to community detection techniques based on the edge-independence assumption. Our findings highlight the benefits of incorporating edge- and label-dependence in higher-order modeling and data analysis, and point to several directions for future work.
item.dc:creator: Violet Ross, Francis Cataldo, Philip S. Chodrow

item.title: Emergence and Collapse of Leader-Follower Flocks through Phantom Targets: Surprise Nullification in Bayesian and Inverse Bayesian Inference
item.description: arXiv:2611.22190v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In Bayesian and inverse Bayesian (BIB) inference, surprise nullification expands belief and likelihood variances by a common factor while preserving the variance-ratio update rule of standard Bayesian inference. This can weaken confidence in existing beliefs without increasing the learning rate. We studied collective motion in three agents that predicted one another's positions using BIB inference and moved toward those predictions, without alignment rules or designated leaders. Across 100 trials, the agents repeatedly formed and dissolved leader-follower flocks. Three leadership criteria identified the same agent in 79% of eligible flocks, with different agents leading different flocks. Flocks typically formed when an agent nearly stopped incorporating observations of a partner (a link cut) and pursued a predicted position detached from reality (a phantom target). Link cuts arose from two consecutive redrawings of the likelihood variance (resets): the first sharply reduced belief variance, and the second raised the likelihood-to-belief variance ratio, suppressing learning. The resulting straight motion attracted followers. Flocks collapsed when the returning phantom target balanced the leader's forward and backward attractions; link recovery generally followed collapse. Without nullification, cuts rarely recovered, whereas expanding only belief variance caused recovery within a few steps. Joint expansion allowed cuts to persist while belief uncertainty grew and enabled later recovery through likelihood-variance resets. Thus, surprise nullification reconciles the persistence and recovery of inaccurate predictions, enabling transient collective order without prescribed leadership.
item.dc:creator: Shuji Shinohara, Daiki Morita, Yoshihiro Nakajima, Takeshi Takano, Masakazu Higuchi, Ung-il Chung, Yukio-Pegio Gunji
